title: Miserere mei, Deus
hook: A psalm for the Sistine Chapel, with a high note that floats above everything.

painting.title: Pope Pius VII in the Sistine Chapel
painting.pairingNote: A papal service in the Sistine Chapel, with Michelangelo’s Last Judgment on the end wall: the room the Miserere was written for, where the Pope’s choir sang it in Holy Week for generations.

facts: Gregorio Allegri, a singer in the Pope’s choir, wrote this setting of Psalm 51, “Have mercy on me, O God”, in the 1630s, some time before 1638. It was written for the Sistine Chapel in Rome and sung there during the services of Holy Week.

The written music is simple: slow chords, verse after verse, alternating with [[plainchant|plainchant]]. What made it famous were the ornaments the papal singers added, a tradition passed on by ear and closely guarded.

The best-known story is about Mozart. In April 1770, aged fourteen, he heard the Miserere in Rome and wrote it down from memory. The only source is a letter from his father. Historians doubt parts of the story, since copies of the music were already known outside the Vatican; it had been sung in London since about 1735.

The famous high note, a top C for a solo soprano, is not Allegri’s. It comes from a version published in 1880 and became famous through an English edition of 1951 and a 1963 recording by the choir of King’s College, Cambridge.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a full choir, a single chanting voice and a distant solo quartet take turns, verse by verse, until both choirs join for the last verse.

movements.heading: Miserere mei, Deus
movements.title: Miserere mei, Deus
movements.summary: Twenty verses of the psalm, sung by three groups in turn: a five-voice choir, a single voice singing plainchant, and a four-voice solo quartet whose top line climbs to the high C. For the last verse both choirs sing together, nine voices in all.

mainIdeas.name: The choir
mainIdeas.description: five voices singing slow, plain chords.

mainIdeas.name: The chant
mainIdeas.description: one man’s voice alone, singing the words to a simple, ancient melody.

mainIdeas.name: The quartet
mainIdeas.description: four solo voices, placed further away, with the top soprano floating up to a very high note and down again in ornamental turns.

stops.hear: The full choir, slow and quiet, in rich chords
One male voice alone, singing a simple melody
Four voices from further away; the highest climbs to a very high note and holds it
stops.happening: Verse 3, the solo quartet, with the high C

stops.hear: After another chanted verse, the full choir again
stops.happening: Verse 5. The cycle begins again: choir, chant, quartet, chant

stops.hear: The solo quartet and the high note again
The quartet for the last time
Both groups sing together, a fuller sound than before, then a long, quiet close

notice: The high C comes five times, once in each quartet verse. Each time, listen for how the soprano reaches it and how slowly she comes down.
Between the high notes, the chanted verses are very plain. The contrast is part of the effect.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The album has the Miserere twice. The times here follow the first track, the familiar version with the high C sung by Deborah Roberts. The last track adds further ornaments that Roberts developed over many years of performing the piece. The solo quartet was placed at a distance to suggest the sound of the singers in the Sistine Chapel, and Andrew Carwood sings the chant.

threads.title: Three groups
threads.body: The piece is a conversation between the full choir, the single chanting voice and the distant quartet.

threads.title: Ornament over plain chords
threads.body: The written music is simple; the beauty comes from the decoration that singers added over generations.
